It’s Hard to Build a Home for Under $1 Million—But It Isn’t Impossible
 
Plus, a trip to Italy’s Costa Smeralda and three real-estate pros share some over-the-top asks from their clients
 
By Kerry Barger
 
 
Phillip and Alexa Falconer in their sunken living room with their dogs Amber, left, and Barley. JAKE PARRISH FOR WSJ
 

This is an edition of the WSJ Homes newsletter, a weekly guide to luxurious properties, celebrity homes, interior design and the housing market. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

We read plenty about homeowner nonnegotiables, but our series on building a custom home for under $1 million reveals the cuts people have made to stay on budget, too.

 

Take Alexa and Phillip Falconer. They just finished building a two-bedroom modern house that came in right on budget at $861,000. The couple originally wanted zinc exterior panels for fire protection, but when those were quoted at $175,000, they opted for corrugated metal at half the cost. Instead of hiring a professional landscaper, they are tackling the grounds themselves. And while Alexa had her heart set on a $15,000 stone bathtub, she passed after realizing it was too big for the space and too expensive to customize.

 

“The trick is to not get your heart set on a specific material or look, as long as you can achieve the same feeling with an alternative,” Phillip says.

 
 
JAKE PARRISH, THE WALL STREET JOURNAL
 

In our first story of the series, we explored how two retirees cut down on square footage by skipping a garage and eliminating hallways. Read about the $700,000 house here.

 

We take a trip to Italy’s Costa Smeralda on Sardinia’s jagged northeast coast known for its sandy beaches, turquoise waters and yachting culture. Home buyers, which now include Americans, are drawn to the area’s natural beauty, Blue Zone status and an expanded season that once lasted just weeks or days.

 

And finally, we have a fun one on some of the more over-the-top requests that real-estate agents have fielded from their clients. My personal favorite: A pool deck that was 100% private so the homeowners could host skinny-dipping parties.

 
 
 

These Remote Workers Built a $861,000 Custom Home Without Blowing Their Budget

 
 
JAKE PARRISH FOR WSJ
 

To keep their Washington vacation property under $1 million, the couple spread the square footage across two levels and handled the landscaping themselves.

Urinals, Skinny-Dipping Pools and Other Wild Home Buyer Must-Haves

 
 
MAR HERNANDEZ FOR WSJ
 

“I’ve been practicing real estate for 15 years, and no one has ever requested a urinal before.” We asked three agents about their clients’ most over-the-top must-haves.

 
 
 

What’s the Deal?

 
 
CLARITY NW
 

A senior living executive is listing his Lake Washington home for $71 million, which would set a record for the Pacific Northwest if it fetches close to its asking price.

 

In California, a roughly 15,200-square-foot house with a curved roof and English timber architecture is relisting for $15.45 million. The home’s “fantasyland” aesthetic was inspired by its original owner’s love of Disney.

 

Want to see more deals? Sign up for our Mansion Deals email alert to have the biggest and best luxury home sales and listings delivered to your inbox.

 
 
 

The Luxe Life

 
 
RYAN THOMAS LAY
 

Before making her debut as a full-time cast member in 2023 on the Bravo reality show “The Real Housewives of Atlanta,” Shamea Morton spent $1.5 million to ensure that her house was camera-ready.

 

Dave Winfield was drafted by the Orioles right out of high school, but attended college instead. “Ma had instilled in us the importance of education, but I also felt my athletic value would rise.”

 
 
 

House of the Week

 
 
JPM REAL ESTATE PHOTOGRAPHY
 

We head to Texas Hill Country for WSJ’s House of the Week, where a podcaster and doula set up shop inside a Modernist compound with a fan-shaped roof. The property offers access to the Pedernales River and features a grotto-style saltwater pool with a hidden cave, along with a separate hot tub tucked beneath a tree canopy.

 
 
 

Your Home

 

• With mortgage rates on the cusp of topping 7% for the fifth year in a row, it might be time to stop waiting for lower rates to put your home on the market.

 

• Housing starts fell in August as home-building activity declined.

 

• U.S. mortgage rates are closing in on 7% for the first time since January 2025, threatening to further discourage prospective home buyers.
